briefs.thyroid:
Thyroid Disease in an Adult

thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) first, then uptake splits making from leaking · levothyroxine recheck timing and its exceptions · the 30% rule and pregnancy-specific normsIs the gland making or leaking, has the TSH had 6 to 8 weeks to settle, and is she pregnant right now?

DiagnosisLevothyroxinePregnancyPractice
Bottom line

Check TSH first, then T4 (thyroxine):

  • Thyrotoxicosis: low TSH with high T4. Radioactive iodine uptake is the next step, but not in a woman who is pregnant (except a molar pregnancy) or breastfeeding.
  • Primary hypothyroidism: high TSH with low T4.
  • Central hypothyroidism: both low, or a normal TSH with a low T4; check cortisol first.
  • High uptake: the gland is making hormone.
  • Low uptake: the hormone is leaking from the gland or is exogenous; antithyroid drugs are useless there.
  • Levothyroxine: TSH lags a dose change by 6 to 8 weeks; pregnancy is the exception, where the dose goes up before the TSH moves.
Diagnosis
Thyroid disease: the differential
DiagnosisThe pictureLabs and uptakeTreatment
Graves diseaseYoung woman; the most common hyperthyroidism; diffuse goiter, with or without a bruit; exophthalmos and pretibial myxedema: Graves onlyTSH-receptor antibodies positive; diffuse high uptakeMethimazole, or propylthiouracil (PTU) in the first trimester; radioactive iodine; or surgery
Toxic multinodular goiter (Plummer)Elderly, longstanding lumpy goiter; apathetic hyperthyroidism: new atrial fibrillation, weight loss, depressionPatchy multifocal hot nodulesRadioactive iodine or surgery; autonomous nodules, not a thyroiditis
Toxic adenomaSingle autonomous noduleOne hot nodule, rest coldRadioactive iodine or lobectomy; hot nodules are almost never cancer
Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditisPost-viral: painful, tender gland after a viral upper respiratory infection; pain to the jaw or earHigh erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), low uptake; hyper, then hypo, then recoveryNonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), with or without steroids; the only painful thyrotoxicosis
Painless or postpartum thyroiditisPainless small goiter; classically 2 to 6 months postpartumThyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies positive, low uptake, normal ESRBeta-blocker only: nothing is being made
Hashimoto thyroiditisThe most common hypothyroidism; firm, rubbery goiter; may have a brief hashitoxicosisAnti-TPO; Hürthle cells, germinal centersLevothyroxine; a rapidly enlarging gland points to B-cell lymphoma
Factitious thyrotoxicosisSupplements or healthcare access; no goiterLow uptake and low thyroglobulinStop the hormone; thyroglobulin is high when a gland leaks
Riedel thyroiditis, IgG4 (immunoglobulin G subclass 4)-relatedRock-hard, fixed, painless; mimics anaplastic carcinomaFibrosis, IgG4 plasma cellsSteroids or tamoxifen; young and hard: Riedel; old: anaplastic
Thyroid storm (emergency)Fever, tachyarrhythmia and delirium; precipitant: surgery, infection, iodine loadClinical diagnosis: do not wait for labsBeta-blocker, then PTU, then iodine at least 1 hour later, then steroids (iodine first fuels synthesis)
Central hypothyroidismHypothyroid with other pituitary deficits; after Sheehan syndrome, a mass or apoplexyTSH low or normal with a low T4Titrate to free T4, not TSH; screen cortisol first
Levothyroxine titration
Recheck timing and its exceptions Recheck interval – TSH lags dose changes by 6 to 8 weeks; earlier values are untrustworthy. At 8 weeks it is reliable: a TSH of 9.5 then means the dose is genuinely inadequate, so increase it · Rechecked too soon – under 6 weeks after a change: recheck in 6 weeks, not a dose change (outside pregnancy; in pregnancy, TSH may be rechecked 4 to 6 weeks after a change) · TSH stays high despite escalating doses – adherence, then absorption: empty stomach; iron, calcium, proton pump inhibitors and cholestyramine bind it; consider celiac disease · Elderly or coronary artery disease – start low, go slow (25 to 50 µg) to avoid angina or arrhythmia · Central hypothyroidism – titrate to free T4; TSH is the broken variable · Subclinical hypothyroidism – high TSH, normal T4: treat if TSH is over 10, TPO-positive, pregnant, or symptomatic · Pregnancy – levothyroxine requirements frequently increase, usually by 25 to 50%; increase the dose as soon as pregnancy is confirmed
Hypothyroidism in pregnancy

Estrogen raises thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG). β-hCG (beta human chorionic gonadotropin) shares an alpha subunit with TSH and stimulates the TSH receptor. As a result, a normal pregnancy makes more thyroxine on its own; a patient with pre-existing hypothyroidism cannot up-regulate.

The 30% rule Dose rule – increase levothyroxine by 20 to 30% (for example, two extra daily doses a week) as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, even with a currently normal TSH; do not wait for the TSH to rise · Monitoring – TSH may be checked at confirmation, approximately every 4 weeks during the first half of pregnancy, at least once in the third trimester, and 4 to 6 weeks after any dose change, using pregnancy-specific norms; target a TSH between the lower limit of the reference range and 2.5 mU/L. Free T4 (analog assay) is an appropriate marker in the first half of pregnancy · Mechanism – estrogen raises TBG, so more hormone is needed to saturate binding sites; as pregnancy progresses, transfer of maternal T4 to the fetus and T4 degradation by placental type 3 deiodinase add to the need. Separately, β-hCG cross-stimulates the TSH receptor, which lowers TSH in the first trimester · Drug – levothyroxine; T3 (triiodothyronine), given as liothyronine, is never the right drug in pregnancy · Graves disease in pregnancy – PTU is the recommended drug in the first trimester (American Thyroid Association, 2017); whether to switch to methimazole after it is a clinical choice; never radioactive iodine
Thyroid labs in normal first-trimester pregnancy
HormoneChangeInterpretation
Total T4IncreasedPhysiologic: TBG excess binds more hormone
Free T4Unchanged or mildly increasedThe value to trust in the first half of pregnancy
TSHDecreasedβ-hCG cross-reactivity: not hyperthyroidism
Practice
  1. 32-year-old woman has 6 weeks of heat intolerance and tremor small, nontender goiter no eye signs; no pretibial skin change Not breastfeeding; no neck pain or recent illness HR 104/min · TSH low · free T4 high · urine pregnancy test negative → Radioactive iodine uptake → thyrotoxicosis with no sign that names the cause, in a woman who is neither pregnant nor breastfeeding: radioactive iodine uptake splits a gland making hormone (high uptake) from one leaking it or exogenous hormone (low uptake). Thyroid ultrasound shows structure, not function, and cannot split making from leaking; fine-needle aspiration is for a cold nodule
  2. 44-year-old woman with hypothyroidism returns for a dose check Started levothyroxine 8 weeks ago; takes it daily on an empty stomach still tired; no palpitations HR 62/min · BP 118/76 mm Hg · TSH 9.5 mU/L → Increase the dose → TSH lags dose changes by 6 to 8 weeks; at 8 weeks it is reliable, so a TSH of 9.5 means the dose is genuinely inadequate: increase it. Rechecking in 6 weeks is the answer only for a value drawn too soon
  3. 32-year-old woman has 3 months of weight loss and palpitations diffuse goiter with a bruit proptosis of both eyes No neck pain HR 112/min · BP 138/70 mm Hg · TSH low · free T4 high → Graves disease → a diffuse goiter with a bruit and proptosis: proptosis and pretibial myxedema occur in Graves disease only, so they make the diagnosis, and uptake is diffusely high. Toxic multinodular goiter is a lumpy gland in an older patient with patchy uptake; subacute thyroiditis is painful, with low uptake
  4. 28-year-old woman with hypothyroidism has a positive home pregnancy test On a stable levothyroxine dose for 3 years feels well; no palpitations or fatigue HR 74/min · BP 112/70 mm Hg · TSH 1.8 mU/L → Increase the dose by about 30% now → a patient with pre-existing hypothyroidism cannot up-regulate, so increase levothyroxine by 20 to 30% (for example, two extra daily doses a week) as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, even with a currently normal TSH, then TSH may be rechecked in about 4 weeks. Waiting until the TSH rises is the titration rule in the wrong slot; liothyronine is never the right drug in pregnancy
  5. 40-year-old woman has 1 week of neck pain radiating to the jaw Sore throat 3 weeks ago thyroid painful and very tender uptake scan: low uptake T 37.9 °C · HR 106/min · TSH low · ESR 88 mm/h → Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis → a painful, tender gland after a viral upper respiratory infection, with pain to the jaw, a high ESR and low uptake: the only painful thyrotoxicosis. It runs hyper, then hypo, then recovery; treat with NSAIDs, with or without steroids. Hashimoto thyroiditis is a firm, rubbery goiter with anti-TPO antibodies; painless thyroiditis has a normal ESR
  6. 44-year-old woman with hypothyroidism has her TSH rechecked Her levothyroxine dose was increased 3 weeks ago takes each dose on an empty stomach feels better; not pregnant HR 66/min · BP 120/78 mm Hg · TSH 8 mU/L → Make no change → make no change and recheck in 6 weeks: outside pregnancy, a TSH rechecked under 6 weeks after a change is untrustworthy, because it lags dose changes by 6 to 8 weeks. A dose change now reacts to a value that has not settled
  7. 55-year-old woman with untreated hyperthyroidism is brought in for agitation Received iodinated contrast for imaging 3 days ago confused and diaphoretic no neck stiffness; lungs clear T 40.0 °C · atrial fibrillation, HR 156/min · BP 150/60 mm Hg → Thyroid storm → fever, tachyarrhythmia and delirium in a thyrotoxic patient after an iodine load: a clinical diagnosis, so treatment does not wait for labs. Give a beta-blocker, then a thionamide (PTU), then iodine at least 1 hour later, then steroids. Graves disease without storm lacks the fever and delirium. Sepsis has no evident source (lungs clear, no neck stiffness), while untreated hyperthyroidism after an iodine load, a known storm precipitant, explains the whole picture
  8. 30-year-old woman in her first pregnancy is seen at 9 weeks' gestation Asymptomatic apart from mild morning nausea no goiter; no eye signs HR 84/min · TSH 0.3 mU/L · total T4 elevated · free T4 high-normal → Normal pregnancy physiology → in a normal first trimester, total T4 rises because excess thyroxine-binding globulin binds more hormone, and TSH falls from β-hCG cross-reactivity: physiology, not hyperthyroidism, so no treatment. Free T4 is the value to trust, and it distinguishes physiology from Graves disease
  9. 45-year-old woman has 6 months of fatigue, weight gain and constipation firm, rubbery, nontender goiter Feels cold when others are comfortable positive TPO antibodies HR 58/min · TSH high · free T4 low → Hashimoto thyroiditis → a firm, rubbery goiter with anti-TPO antibodies and primary hypothyroidism is the most common hypothyroidism; treat with levothyroxine. Hürthle cells and germinal centers are its histology. Subacute thyroiditis is painful; Riedel thyroiditis is rock-hard, fixed and painless
  10. 44-year-old woman with hypothyroidism has a persistently high TSH Takes levothyroxine each morning together with her calcium supplement reports taking every dose; no other medications HR 60/min · BP 118/74 mm Hg · TSH 7.8 mU/L → Separate them by 4 hours → a TSH that stays high despite the dose: adherence first, then absorption. Iron, calcium, proton pump inhibitors and cholestyramine bind levothyroxine, so it is taken on an empty stomach: separate the calcium from it by 4 hours rather than raising the dose. Consider celiac disease when absorption is the problem
  11. 30-year-old woman has 3 weeks of palpitations and anxiety Delivered 3 months ago; not breastfeeding small, painless, nontender goiter; no eye signs uptake scan: low uptake HR 108/min · BP 124/76 mm Hg · TSH low · free T4 high → Postpartum thyroiditis → painless thyrotoxicosis 2 to 6 months postpartum with low uptake; TPO antibodies are typically positive and the ESR normal. Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis is painful and tender; a toxic adenoma is one hot nodule with the rest cold
  12. 28-year-old woman at 8 weeks' gestation was diagnosed with Graves disease today diffuse goiter with a bruit; mild proptosis First pregnancy; no prior thyroid treatment HR 112/min · BP 128/72 mm Hg · TSH low · free T4 high → Propylthiouracil → PTU is the recommended drug in the first trimester (American Thyroid Association, 2017), not methimazole, because PTU generally carries a lower risk of birth defects than methimazole; whether to switch to methimazole after it is a clinical choice. Radioactive iodine is never an option in pregnancy
  13. 44-year-old woman on levothyroxine has 3 weeks of palpitations Dose increased 10 weeks ago fine tremor; warm, moist skin No new medications or supplements HR 108/min · BP 132/70 mm Hg · TSH 0.05 mU/L → Decrease the dose → a TSH of 0.05 with palpitations, drawn after the 6 to 8 week lag, is a reliable value: the dose is too high, so decrease it ⚠︎. Adding a beta-blocker and continuing leaves the dose too high ⚠︎
  14. 28-year-old woman, a nurse, has 2 months of palpitations and weight loss no goiter; thyroid nontender No recent pregnancy or neck pain uptake scan: low uptake HR 110/min · TSH low · free T4 high · thyroglobulin low → Factitious thyrotoxicosis → low uptake with a low thyroglobulin and no goiter is exogenous hormone (supplements or healthcare access): stop the hormone. Thyroglobulin is high when an inflamed gland leaks, as in painless thyroiditis; a toxic adenoma is one hot nodule
  15. 31-year-old woman with hypothyroidism is 6 weeks pregnant Her levothyroxine dose was increased today She asks when her thyroid tests will be repeated mild nausea; no palpitations HR 76/min · BP 110/68 mm Hg → TSH in 4 weeks → TSH may be checked approximately every 4 weeks during the first half of pregnancy and 4 to 6 weeks after any dose change, using pregnancy-specific norms, with a target between the lower limit of the reference range and 2.5 mU/L. The next-trimester visit is too late for a dose changed today, and weekly testing is far more often than the roughly 4-week schedule
  16. 55-year-old woman is delirious the day after a hip fracture repair Graves disease diagnosed 3 years ago agitated, diaphoretic, tremulous T 40.0 °C · atrial fibrillation, HR 160/min · BP 146/58 mm Hg → Beta-blocker → thyroid storm after surgery: the beta-blocker comes first, then PTU, then iodine at least 1 hour later, then steroids. Potassium iodide given first fuels hormone synthesis
  17. 78-year-old woman has new primary hypothyroidism Coronary artery disease with stable angina; stent 2 years ago fatigue, dry skin, constipation HR 56/min · BP 134/80 mm Hg · TSH 14 mU/L · free T4 low → Start low and titrate slowly → elderly or with coronary artery disease: start low and go slow (25 to 50 µg) to avoid angina or arrhythmia
  18. 68-year-old woman has 2 months of weight loss and low mood Neck swelling for many years irregular, multinodular gland; no eye signs uptake scan: patchy, several hot areas HR 104/min, irregularly irregular · TSH low → Toxic multinodular goiter → an elderly patient with a longstanding, lumpy goiter and patchy multifocal hot nodules: autonomous nodules, not a thyroiditis, often with apathetic hyperthyroidism (new atrial fibrillation, weight loss, depression). Treat with radioactive iodine or surgery. Graves disease takes up diffusely; a toxic adenoma is one hot nodule with the rest cold
  19. 27-year-old woman with hypothyroidism plans to conceive in 6 months Takes liothyronine twice daily palpitations some afternoons; tired by evening No other medications HR 82/min · BP 114/70 mm Hg · TSH 2.4 mU/L → Switch to levothyroxine before conception → T3 has a short half-life with wide level swings, and liothyronine is never the right drug in pregnancy: switch to levothyroxine before conception. Adding levothyroxine keeps the liothyronine
  20. 30-year-old woman has palpitations 3 months after delivery small, painless goiter positive TPO antibodies low radioactive iodine uptake Not breastfeeding; no neck pain or fever HR 112/min · BP 122/74 mm Hg · TSH low · free T4 high → Beta-blocker alone → low uptake means nothing is being made, so antithyroid drugs such as methimazole are useless: a beta-blocker only, for the symptoms
  21. 44-year-old woman on levothyroxine for hypothyroidism has a positive home pregnancy test Dose stable for 2 years; TSH normal 6 months ago feels well; mild breast tenderness HR 72/min · BP 116/72 mm Hg → Increase the dose by about 30% and recheck → levothyroxine requirements frequently increase in pregnancy, usually by 25 to 50%: increase the dose as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, by 20 to 30% (for example, two extra daily doses a week), and TSH may be rechecked in about 4 weeks, without waiting for the TSH to rise. Untreated maternal hypothyroidism risks impaired fetal neurodevelopment
  22. 29-year-old woman with hypothyroidism is 10 weeks pregnant Her levothyroxine dose was raised when pregnancy was confirmed total T4 elevated; free T4 normal HR 78/min · BP 112/70 mm Hg · TSH 2.0 mU/L → Estrogen-induced rise in thyroxine-binding globulin → estrogen raises thyroxine-binding globulin, so more hormone is needed to saturate binding sites; as pregnancy progresses, transfer of maternal T4 to the fetus and T4 degradation by placental type 3 deiodinase add to the need. The added T4 degradation the guideline names is placental (type 3 deiodinase) and grows as pregnancy progresses; at 10 weeks the rise in thyroxine-binding globulin is the main driver. β-hCG cross-stimulates the TSH receptor, which is why TSH falls in the first trimester, not why the dose rises ⚠︎
Paired pearls Lid lag and stare occur in any thyrotoxicosis (sympathetic); proptosis and pretibial myxedema occur in Graves only. A hot nodule is almost never cancer; a cold nodule needs fine-needle aspiration. Nodule workup starts with TSH: if low, get an uptake scan; if normal or high, get an ultrasound, then fine-needle aspiration.
Pregnancy pearls Untreated maternal hypothyroidism risks impaired fetal neurodevelopment, because the fetus depends on maternal T4 early. A low TSH with a high total T4 in the first trimester is physiology, not Graves; free T4 distinguishes the two.
Common wrong answers Antithyroid workup for a TSH of 0.3 in early pregnancy: β-hCG cross-reactivity explains the low TSH. “Recheck in 6 to 8 weeks” at conception: correct as a titration rule, but pregnancy is the one setting where acting first is right.
Pairs with Part I Congenital Hypothyroidism is the neonatal version, where the TSH direction and the neck locate the defect.
Transferable rule

Apply an exception to the standard titration rule only when its trigger condition is actually present; otherwise, follow the standard rule. When physiology predictably outruns a fixed drug dose, adjust the dose pre-emptively; do not recheck and react, although that approach is correct in every other setting.
